the-design-method-and-estimation.r: A candidate started drawing boxes before asking about load, and the design collapsed when the interviewer mentioned a hundred thousand requests per second. Starting with requirements and a quick estimate of load and storage would have shaped every later choice.
the-design-method-and-estimation.x: Estimates are for ruling things out, not for precision. State assumptions, find the dominant cost and let it drive the design. Revisit the numbers when a decision is close.

caching-without-stampedes.r: A popular cached item expired and thousands of requests hit the database together, taking it down. Staggering expiry, letting one request refresh while others served the old value, and caching misses briefly stopped the stampede.
caching-without-stampedes.x: Every cache is a consistency decision. Plan for cold starts, hot keys, invalidation and failure of the cache itself, and ensure the backend can survive without it.

queues-retries-and-idempotency.r: A payment message was delivered twice after a timeout and a customer was charged twice. An idempotency key stored with the result made the second delivery harmless.
queues-retries-and-idempotency.x: At-least-once delivery is the realistic default, so make consumers idempotent. Bound retries, add backoff with jitter, use dead-letter queues and watch queue depth as a signal.

consistency-and-availability-in-practice.r: During a network partition, a system had to choose between refusing writes and accepting possibly conflicting ones. The team had decided in advance which data needed strict consistency and which could be reconciled later.
consistency-and-availability-in-practice.x: The trade-off is per operation, not per system. Define the guarantee users need, state what happens during partitions and latency, and test those paths.

quorum-leaders-and-split-brain.r: A cluster split in two and both halves elected a leader, accepting conflicting writes. Requiring a majority quorum meant only one side could continue.
quorum-leaders-and-split-brain.x: Majorities prevent split brain but cost availability when you lose too many nodes. Use an odd number across failure domains, fence old leaders and test partitions.

clocks-time-and-ordering.r: Events from two servers were ordered by their clocks, and a skew of a few hundred milliseconds put a reply before its request. Using logical ordering or a single sequence source fixed the data.
clocks-time-and-ordering.x: Wall clocks drift and jump. Use monotonic clocks for durations, logical clocks or sequence numbers for order, and treat time-based locks and leases with suspicion.

partitioning-sharding-and-consistent-has.r: A system sharded by customer and one huge customer overloaded a single shard. Splitting that customer's data across shards and choosing a better key spread the load.
partitioning-sharding-and-consistent-has.x: Choose the key from access patterns, expect skew and plan rebalancing before you need it. Resharding is hard, so pick a scheme that moves little data when nodes change.

storage-engines-and-replication-topologi.r: A write-heavy workload slowed down on a B-tree store with many random writes. A log-structured engine suited it better, at the cost of compaction work and read amplification.
storage-engines-and-replication-topologi.x: Match the engine and replication topology to the read and write mix. Understand write amplification, replication lag and what happens to durability on each failure.

backup-restore-and-object-storage-design.r: A team had backups in the same account and region as the data, and an account compromise deleted both. Copies in a separate account with immutability made recovery possible.
backup-restore-and-object-storage-design.x: Design restore first: time, point, access, and where the copies live. Test restores regularly and protect backups from the same failure that harms the primary.

failure-domains-cells-and-bulkheads.r: One noisy customer exhausted shared resources and affected everyone. Splitting the platform into cells limited each failure to a fraction of customers.
failure-domains-cells-and-bulkheads.x: Define failure domains explicitly and make dependencies respect them. Cells cost efficiency and operational effort; weigh that against the blast radius you remove.

blast-radius-and-shuffle-sharding.r: A bad request pattern from one client took out the servers it hit. With shuffle sharding, each client used a small random subset of servers, so one client could harm only a tiny share of others.
blast-radius-and-shuffle-sharding.x: Make blast radius a number you can state, then reduce it with isolation, gradual rollout and sharding of clients. Measure how many customers a single fault could touch.

graceful-degradation-and-circuit-breaker.r: A recommendations service failed and the whole product page failed with it. After adding a breaker and a fallback to a generic list, the page loaded without personalised items during the outage.
graceful-degradation-and-circuit-breaker.x: Decide ahead what each dependency's failure looks like to the user. Test the fallback paths, tune breakers on real traffic and avoid fallbacks that overload other parts.

rate-limiting-and-load-shedding.r: A retry storm from clients turned a short slowdown into a long outage. Rate limiting per client and shedding low-priority work first kept the core service up while load subsided.
rate-limiting-and-load-shedding.x: Overload needs a plan: limits, priorities, queues with bounds and honest errors that tell clients to back off. Protect the service by rejecting early and cheaply.

multi-region-and-global-traffic.r: A company ran in two regions but a shared database sat in one, so a regional outage still took everything down. Moving to a design where each region could serve independently removed that hidden single point.
multi-region-and-global-traffic.x: Active-active gives resilience and complexity: data conflicts, latency and cost. Decide the consistency you need, how traffic fails over, and test the failover under load.

config-and-control-plane-change-safety.r: A configuration change was pushed to every region at once and had a typo that broke all of them. Rolling it out gradually with validation and automatic rollback would have caught it in the first small group.
config-and-control-plane-change-safety.x: Treat configuration as code with review, validation, staged rollout and rollback. Keep the data plane working if the control plane is down, and watch for changes that propagate faster than you can stop them.

hidden-dependencies-and-single-points.r: During an outage, a team discovered their recovery tools needed the very system that was down. Mapping dependencies, including for login, DNS and deployment, found others before they bit.
hidden-dependencies-and-single-points.x: List what your service needs to start, to run and to recover, and look for circular ones. A dependency you did not know about is the one that will fail.

observability-by-design.r: A new service launched without meaningful metrics, and its first incident took hours to diagnose. Defining service level indicators and the questions to answer during design put the right signals in from the start.
observability-by-design.x: Decide before launch what you must know when it fails: SLIs, correlation identifiers and dashboards for dependencies. Test the telemetry by simulating a failure.

security-and-identity-by-design.r: Services trusted each other because they were on the same network, and one compromised service reached all of them. Authenticating each call with short-lived credentials limited what an intruder could do.
security-and-identity-by-design.x: Design for least privilege, strong identity for services, encryption and auditability from the start. Retrofitting security is far harder than building it in.

capacity-planning-and-cost-trade-offs.r: A service was sized for peak with a large safety margin and cost twice what it needed to. Measuring real headroom and autoscaling for the daily pattern cut cost while keeping a safe margin.
capacity-planning-and-cost-trade-offs.x: Capacity is a trade between cost and risk. Plan headroom from measurement, load-test the limits, and revisit the plan after launches. Cost is a design constraint, not an afterthought.

worked-design-global-api-at-four-nines.r: To reach a 99.99 percent target, a team found that the SLO could not be higher than their dependencies allowed. They added regional independence and graceful degradation to meet it.
worked-design-global-api-at-four-nines.x: Work backwards from the error budget: roughly four minutes a month. Every dependency, deploy and failover consumes it, so design the deployment and rollback process as carefully as the architecture.

worked-design-the-status-page-that-survi.r: A status page hosted on the same infrastructure as the product went down with it, and customers had no information. Hosting it independently on a different provider kept updates flowing.
worked-design-the-status-page-that-survi.x: A system for communicating during outages must not depend on the thing that fails. Keep it simple, static where possible and test updating it under degraded conditions.

worked-design-a-url-shortener.r: A short link service looked simple until estimates showed reads outnumbered writes a hundred to one. Caching hot links and generating IDs without coordination made it fast and cheap.
worked-design-a-url-shortener.x: Estimate first, then decide: ID generation, storage, caching, redirects, abuse and analytics. A simple design can still hide hard problems such as expiry, deletion and malicious links.

worked-design-a-rate-limiter-service.r: A limiter built on one shared counter became a bottleneck and single point of failure. Local counters with periodic sync gave approximate limits with far better resilience.
worked-design-a-rate-limiter-service.x: Exactness has a cost. Decide how accurate limits must be, what happens when the limiter is down (fail open or closed) and how clients learn their limits.

worked-design-a-notification-fan-out-sys.r: A single event had to reach millions of users and the sender overwhelmed downstream providers. Queues, batching, per-provider rate limits and priority lanes made delivery steady.
worked-design-a-notification-fan-out-sys.x: Fan-out multiplies load, so design for backpressure, retries, deduplication and user preferences. Separate urgent from bulk and measure delivery time as well as success.

worked-design-a-metrics-and-log-pipeline.r: A pipeline lost data during a traffic spike because it had no buffering. Adding a durable queue between collectors and storage preserved data and allowed catching up afterwards.
worked-design-a-metrics-and-log-pipeline.x: Ingest, buffer, process and store with clear limits at each stage. Control cardinality and retention, and decide what you drop first under pressure.

worked-design-a-multi-tenant-kubernetes-.r: Teams sharing a cluster interfered with each other until quotas, network policies and separate node pools gave each a safe space. Some teams with strict needs moved to their own clusters.
worked-design-a-multi-tenant-kubernetes-.x: Multi-tenancy is a spectrum of isolation versus cost. Decide the tenant model, enforce it with policy, and plan upgrades, observability and cost reporting per tenant.

worked-design-an-authoritative-dns-servi.r: A DNS provider outage made many sites unreachable even though their servers were fine. Using two independent providers for authoritative service removed that single point of failure.
worked-design-an-authoritative-dns-servi.x: DNS is high-fan-in and hard to change quickly. Plan redundancy across providers, safe change processes, caching behaviour and attack protection.
